doc.title: JJ Johnson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Other black film composers; observing Quincy and Lalo's sessions
summary: Baker asks about Benny Carter, Quincy and Oliver Nelson; Johnson played trombone on Quincy and Lalo's calls.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Did you have much contact with some of the other black composers [in Hollywood] like Benny [Carter]? Benny was trying his damnedest not get involved with the actual orchestration so [he] wouldn’t get labeled [as only an orchestrator]. But Benny, Quincy, Coleridge-Taylor Perkinson . . .
I don’t recall that Oliver ever had a chance to do a feature film. His forte was mostly television. He may have done one.
He did one with Lena Horne and Yul Brynner. I can’t remember what it was called. [Death of a Gunfighter]
I think it was The Gunfighter or something like that. But that was his only feature [film].
That’s it. Death of a Gunfighter.

Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah. Death of a Gunfighter, yeah. I didn’t come into contact too much, other than with Quincy. I ran into Quincy once, and played on a couple of his film calls in the trombone section.
I got to observe at close range . . .

. . . how he operated as a composer on a film project. One comes to mind. Ohhh. I can’t remember what it was now 'cause I played on two or three of Quincy’s film scores. I played on a couple of Lalo’s film scores in the trombone section. [It] was good to get to observe how they dealt with a film score.
And look at it from inside, too.
Oh, yes, yes. [To] look at it from the standpoint of the players. It was really an education.
